title: Self-selecting Fluid Intake while Maintaining High Carbohydrate Availability Does not Impair Half-marathon Performance
authors: Lee MJ, Hammond KM, Vasdev A, Poole KL, Impey SG, Close GL, Morton JP
population: 15 participants who ran three half marathons, finishing in about 110 min, each with high carbohydrate availability (60 g/h from gels in two arms; a 6% carbohydrate drink to guidelines in the third)
findings: Participants drank a 6% carbohydrate solution to guidelines (DRINK) or a non-caloric solution in self-selected volumes with three 20 g glucose gels per hour (G-GEL) or three glucose-fructose gels per hour (GF-GEL).
Fluid intake (1,557, 473 and 404 mL) and body mass loss (0.8, 2.0 and 2.3%) differed between conditions, but race time did not (110.6 +/- 14.4, 110.3 +/- 14.6 and 113.7 +/- 12.8 min).
In G-GEL there was a positive correlation between body mass loss and race time.

Plasma glucose was lower in GF-GEL, and total carbohydrate oxidation (3.2, 3.0 and 2.6 g/min) was lower (P = 0.06); the authors say glucose-fructose mixtures in sub-optimal amounts reduce plasma glucose and total oxidation rates.
limitations: All three arms kept carbohydrate high, so there is no no-carbohydrate arm and the paper cannot show that any rate helps; it shows that 60 g/h from gels was taken at a roughly 110 min half-marathon effort without a change in time between fluid strategies; 15 participants.
implications: At about 110 min (the under-2-hour band) a 60 g/h intake was tolerated and fluid volume did not change race time. This is tolerance data, not a test of benefit, so it does not justify stating a rate for the band.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (IJSM 35:1216-1222). Abstract read on Europe PMC. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
